rankingRules.falseCutoff: by severity descending: gapSeconds = (true pause length) − (time the cut landed), i.e. how much of the pause the speaker still had left; ties broken by longer true pause, then earlier cut, then span key
rankingRules.missedEnd: by severity descending: gapSeconds = (model fire time) − timeout, with "never crossed the threshold at all" = Infinity ranked first (the model gave no signal, so the endpoint came only from the timer); ties broken by span key

gapDefinition.falseCutoff: gtEndMs − decisionEventMs, in seconds: how early the cut landed relative to when the speaker actually resumed
gapDefinition.missedEnd: modelFireMs − timeoutDeadlineMs, in seconds (Infinity when the model never fired)

crossComparison.conclusion: At the fixed point on the merged corpus (710 holds, 416 EoT): the timer baseline cuts 68/710 holds (9.58%) but misses nothing (it fires immediately). Smart Turn cuts 33 (4.65%) and misses 27 (6.49%); turn-1-mini cuts 32 (4.51%) and misses 14 (3.37%). So a pure timer is NOT dominated on the miss side — it never misses — and the models' value is entirely on the cutoff side: they cut roughly 0.51× (Smart Turn) and 0.53× (turn-1-mini) fewer real pauses, and in exchange they give up some endpoint certainty (27 and 14 EoT spans that only the timeout caught). A deployment that would rather wait than interrupt should read that trade as: the model buys back pauses at the price of occasionally falling back to the timer, which is exactly the same fallback the baseline uses unconditionally.
